medical.title: Scientists find the gene that drives T-cell exhaustion, revealing new strategy to improve immune responses
medical.summary: Immunotherapy, which uses a patient's immune system to treat disease, has increased survival for some adults and children with cancer. However, it has had limited success against many pediatric solid tumors, in part because T cells can become functionally impaired or "exhausted." St. Jude Children's Research Hospital scientists published results in Nature showing that the gene ZMYND8 is a major regulator of CD8+ T-cell exhaustion. The results also showed that removing the gene improves antitumor and antiviral responses on its own and may have a synergistic effect with immunotherapy.

medical.title: Appendicitis patients assessed after 72 hours have 48% rupture rate, global data show
medical.summary: A new global study into appendicitis has found major inequalities in care, with some countries having little access to CT imaging or minimally invasive surgery—resulting in poorer patient outcomes.

medical.title: Oral menopausal hormone therapy linked to higher blood clot risk; transdermal treatment shows no overall increase
medical.summary: Current use of oral menopausal hormone therapy (commonly known as hormone replacement therapy or HRT) is associated with an increased risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs regardless of dose or treatment duration, finds a large Danish study published by The BMJ.

medical.title: First map of mouse brain lipids reveals over 500 biochemical zones
medical.summary: The brain is often described in terms of cells and wiring. However, much of it is made of lipids that form the membranes of neurons, wrap nerve fibers with myelin and help brain cells send and receive signals.

medical.title: Childhood cancer survivors' cells repair low-dose radiation damage more efficiently, study finds
medical.summary: A study of how cells repair radiation-induced genetic damage offers clues to why some people develop cancer early in life or more than once. The findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Shorter, gentler exercise programs may ease pain more than tougher workouts
medical.summary: From osteoarthritis to a splitting migraine, when you're experiencing pain, exercise can seem like the last thing you want or think you should do. But according to new Adelaide University research published in PAIN Reports, it could be one of the most effective ways to help ease your symptoms.

medical.title: Study identifies potential RAS inhibitor-immunotherapy strategy for pancreatic cancer
medical.summary: Pancreatic cancer does not respond to most immunotherapies, but RAS inhibitors could alter tumors to make them more sensitive to a novel immunotherapeutic approach. In pancreatic tumors with RAS mutations, RAS inhibitors cause massive cell death and reduce immunosuppression. These changes tend to be temporary because tumors develop resistance to the therapy.

medical.title: Mortality, comorbidity risk increased with generalized pustular psoriasis
medical.summary: Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP) is associated with higher mortality and comorbidity risks than psoriasis vulgaris (PV), according to a study published online Sept. 2 in Frontiers in Immunology. The risks also were higher than those among nonpsoriatic controls.

medical.title: Researchers identify cellular stress-protection system that may help tumors withstand chemotherapy
medical.summary: Many cancer treatments work by exploiting weaknesses in tumor cells, overwhelming their ability to survive, repair damage or continue growing. Yet some cancer cells manage to survive treatment. A new study from Texas A&M University sheds light on one reason why: Some cancer cells have a survival toolkit.

medical.title: Scientists unveil the most detailed and precise map of the mouse motor cortex to date
medical.summary: The brain's motor cortex plans, controls and executes voluntary muscle movements. Whether you're playing catch, writing your name or chewing food, it all points back to this region and its connections to other parts of the brain. Yet despite extensive study, scientists still haven't created a detailed map of how the mouse motor cortex is internally organized. Most brain atlases have divided it into two general regions—primary and secondary—based on differences in connectivity, but this doesn't provide a detailed or consistent picture.

science.title: Hungary detects invasive spotted lanternfly for the first time in the EU
science.summary: An invasive insect linked to major agricultural losses in the U.S. has been detected in the European Union for the first time, Hungary's food safety agency said Thursday.

science.title: Researchers build microscopic DNA 'sails' to pull molecules apart
science.summary: Across every cell in the body, molecules are constantly pulling, gripping and releasing under mechanical strain. That force often decides whether a drug sticks to its target, whether a cell holds its shape or whether a disease takes hold.

science.title: Climate change: Laws and policies must change to prevent future statelessness
science.summary: Australia and other nations should amend laws and practices to address the needs of millions of people expected to move because of climate-related hazards, according to a new report by the Peter McMullin Centre on Statelessness and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

science.title: Q&A: Why should colleges promote student physical activity?
science.summary: Every fall in the United States, millions of young people move to college campuses, away from home for the first time. During this transition, they typically develop new social networks and routines as they learn to live on their own. One of the most important routines college students can intentionally develop is regular physical activity, according to Melissa Bopp, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State.

science.title: 1 in 3 Tucsonans exposed to historic water contamination still report signs of psychological trauma
science.summary: Residents of Tucson's south side might remember drinking from the garden hose and bathing their children in tap water. For years, that water was contaminated with industrial solvents that had leaked into the groundwater their wells drew from.

science.title: How calcium channels in muscle cells open together
science.summary: Every step we take begins with a burst of calcium inside our muscle cells, causing them to contract. To prepare for action, the cells keep calcium locked in an internal compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Studding its membrane are thousands of RyR1 channels—the largest known ion channels—that contain pores that release the calcium. For a muscle to contract properly, RyR1 channels must open synchronously via a mechanism known as "coupled gating." How they accomplish this has been unclear since it was described almost 30 years ago.

science.title: JWST finds early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
science.summary: When the universe was still in its infancy—only 500 million years after the Big Bang, or about 3% of its current age—some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained relatively pristine, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, the primordial ingredients available in the newborn cosmos.

science.title: Bay Area wastewater plants could nearly halve nitrogen cleanup costs by coordinating upgrades
science.summary: Treating polluted water flowing into San Francisco Bay to meet regulatory requirements is going to cost ratepayers money. Exactly how much depends, in large part, on whether the region's wastewater treatment plant operators are willing and able to coordinate infrastructure construction and operation to meet these requirements, according to a Stanford University study published in Nature Water.

science.title: Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
science.summary: U.S. artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Wednesday unveiled the first discovery from its molecular biology lab, a previously unknown enzyme system spotted by its Claude model and touted by the company as proof that AI can speed up basic research.

science.title: Archaeological 'breakthrough' could confirm origins of Paris
science.summary: An ancient wall discovered in central Paris was hailed as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday, as the archaeological find may have settled a long-standing debate about the location of the city's original settlement.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Q&A: Why should colleges promote student physical activity?
mix_items.summary: Every fall in the United States, millions of young people move to college campuses, away from home for the first time. During this transition, they typically develop new social networks and routines as they learn to live on their own. One of the most important routines college students can intentionally develop is regular physical activity, according to Melissa Bopp, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State.

mix_items.title: 1 in 3 Tucsonans exposed to historic water contamination still report signs of psychological trauma
mix_items.summary: Residents of Tucson's south side might remember drinking from the garden hose and bathing their children in tap water. For years, that water was contaminated with industrial solvents that had leaked into the groundwater their wells drew from.

mix_items.title: How calcium channels in muscle cells open together
mix_items.summary: Every step we take begins with a burst of calcium inside our muscle cells, causing them to contract. To prepare for action, the cells keep calcium locked in an internal compartment, the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Studding its membrane are thousands of RyR1 channels—the largest known ion channels—that contain pores that release the calcium. For a muscle to contract properly, RyR1 channels must open synchronously via a mechanism known as "coupled gating." How they accomplish this has been unclear since it was described almost 30 years ago.

mix_items.title: JWST finds early galaxies were already seeding the universe with heavy elements
mix_items.summary: When the universe was still in its infancy—only 500 million years after the Big Bang, or about 3% of its current age—some of the universe's earliest stars and galaxies had already formed. Astronomers have long predicted that much of the gas surrounding these young galaxies must have remained relatively pristine, composed mostly of hydrogen and helium, the primordial ingredients available in the newborn cosmos.

mix_items.title: Bay Area wastewater plants could nearly halve nitrogen cleanup costs by coordinating upgrades
mix_items.summary: Treating polluted water flowing into San Francisco Bay to meet regulatory requirements is going to cost ratepayers money. Exactly how much depends, in large part, on whether the region's wastewater treatment plant operators are willing and able to coordinate infrastructure construction and operation to meet these requirements, according to a Stanford University study published in Nature Water.

mix_items.title: Anthropic touts AI-led biology discovery
mix_items.summary: U.S. artificial intelligence startup Anthropic on Wednesday unveiled the first discovery from its molecular biology lab, a previously unknown enzyme system spotted by its Claude model and touted by the company as proof that AI can speed up basic research.

mix_items.title: Archaeological 'breakthrough' could confirm origins of Paris
mix_items.summary: An ancient wall discovered in central Paris was hailed as a "major breakthrough" on Wednesday, as the archaeological find may have settled a long-standing debate about the location of the city's original settlement.

mix_items.title: Scientists find the gene that drives T-cell exhaustion, revealing new strategy to improve immune responses
mix_items.summary: Immunotherapy, which uses a patient's immune system to treat disease, has increased survival for some adults and children with cancer. However, it has had limited success against many pediatric solid tumors, in part because T cells can become functionally impaired or "exhausted." St. Jude Children's Research Hospital scientists published results in Nature showing that the gene ZMYND8 is a major regulator of CD8+ T-cell exhaustion. The results also showed that removing the gene improves antitumor and antiviral responses on its own and may have a synergistic effect with immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: Appendicitis patients assessed after 72 hours have 48% rupture rate, global data show
mix_items.summary: A new global study into appendicitis has found major inequalities in care, with some countries having little access to CT imaging or minimally invasive surgery—resulting in poorer patient outcomes.

mix_items.title: Oral menopausal hormone therapy linked to higher blood clot risk; transdermal treatment shows no overall increase
mix_items.summary: Current use of oral menopausal hormone therapy (commonly known as hormone replacement therapy or HRT) is associated with an increased risk of blood clots in the legs or lungs regardless of dose or treatment duration, finds a large Danish study published by The BMJ.

mix_items.title: First map of mouse brain lipids reveals over 500 biochemical zones
mix_items.summary: The brain is often described in terms of cells and wiring. However, much of it is made of lipids that form the membranes of neurons, wrap nerve fibers with myelin and help brain cells send and receive signals.

mix_items.title: Childhood cancer survivors' cells repair low-dose radiation damage more efficiently, study finds
mix_items.summary: A study of how cells repair radiation-induced genetic damage offers clues to why some people develop cancer early in life or more than once. The findings were recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Shorter, gentler exercise programs may ease pain more than tougher workouts
mix_items.summary: From osteoarthritis to a splitting migraine, when you're experiencing pain, exercise can seem like the last thing you want or think you should do. But according to new Adelaide University research published in PAIN Reports, it could be one of the most effective ways to help ease your symptoms.

mix_items.title: Study identifies potential RAS inhibitor-immunotherapy strategy for pancreatic cancer
mix_items.summary: Pancreatic cancer does not respond to most immunotherapies, but RAS inhibitors could alter tumors to make them more sensitive to a novel immunotherapeutic approach. In pancreatic tumors with RAS mutations, RAS inhibitors cause massive cell death and reduce immunosuppression. These changes tend to be temporary because tumors develop resistance to the therapy.

mix_items.title: Mortality, comorbidity risk increased with generalized pustular psoriasis
mix_items.summary: Generalized pustular psoriasis (GPP) is associated with higher mortality and comorbidity risks than psoriasis vulgaris (PV), according to a study published online Sept. 2 in Frontiers in Immunology. The risks also were higher than those among nonpsoriatic controls.

mix_items.title: Researchers identify cellular stress-protection system that may help tumors withstand chemotherapy
mix_items.summary: Many cancer treatments work by exploiting weaknesses in tumor cells, overwhelming their ability to survive, repair damage or continue growing. Yet some cancer cells manage to survive treatment. A new study from Texas A&M University sheds light on one reason why: Some cancer cells have a survival toolkit.

mix_items.title: Scientists unveil the most detailed and precise map of the mouse motor cortex to date
mix_items.summary: The brain's motor cortex plans, controls and executes voluntary muscle movements. Whether you're playing catch, writing your name or chewing food, it all points back to this region and its connections to other parts of the brain. Yet despite extensive study, scientists still haven't created a detailed map of how the mouse motor cortex is internally organized. Most brain atlases have divided it into two general regions—primary and secondary—based on differences in connectivity, but this doesn't provide a detailed or consistent picture.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
